articles.title: Obfuscating a Polymorphic JSON Contract: Why [JsonDerivedType] Survives Renaming and TypeNameHandling Does Not
articles.excerpt: Property-level renaming breaks are annoying but shallow: a key comes out wrong, you pin it with [JsonPropertyName], done. Polymorphic serialization is a deeper hazard, because the thing that goes on t…
articles.body: Property-level renaming breaks are annoying but shallow: a key comes out wrong, you pin it with [JsonPropertyName] , done. Polymorphic serialization is a deeper hazard, because the thing that goes on the wire is not a property name — it is the identity of the type itself . Obfuscation exists to destroy that identity. So a polymorphic contract is exactly the place where "renaming broke serialization" stops being a cosmetic wire-name problem and becomes "every document we ever persisted is now unreadable." The good news is that this is entirely a design choice, and the modern .NET design is the safe one.

articles.title: N-central vulnerabilities (Able2Shell): what MSPs should do now
articles.excerpt: This article first appeared on varaxontech.com, where it is kept up to date. The short version On 8 to 9 November 2026 a researcher published working exploit code for flaws in N-able N-central. N-able…
articles.body: This article first appeared on varaxontech.com , where it is kept up to date. The short version On 8 to 9 November 2026 a researcher published working exploit code for flaws in N-able N-central . N-able took hosted N-central offline on 9 November and shipped 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on 10 November with seven CVE fixes. More exploit code followed. N-able says the newer chains need the Legacy API , a setting that is off by default . Make sure it is off, upgrade to HF2, then upgrade every Agent and Probe . A further hotfix, HF3, was still in validation on 14 November. N-able published indicators of compromise on 13 November for servers that had the Legacy API turned on. Check your logs and firewall for them before you call the incident closed.

articles.title: Retrieval Architecture for a Restaurant Menu Assistant: Traceable Delete Semantics
articles.excerpt: The hard part of a restaurant menu assistant is not producing a plausible answer. It is proving that an answer did not come from a dish, price, or allergen note that a manager deleted yesterday. Short…
articles.body: The hard part of a restaurant menu assistant is not producing a plausible answer. It is proving that an answer did not come from a dish, price, or allergen note that a manager deleted yesterday. Short answer: use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a document; treat deletion as a state transition that removes the record from the collection before the assistant can cite it. That choice favors retrieval quality without allowing a slow or stale source to hold the user interface hostage. It also gives a solo builder a clean test: ask the assistant about a removed menu item and inspect the returned identifiers, not just the prose.

articles.title: Recovery Retention: How to Build Secure Password Reset Email with 3 Token Rules
articles.excerpt: A healthtech report email has more behind it than a send charge: retained report bytes, recovery records, delivery evidence, and the integration work needed to replace the sender. In an illustrative w…
articles.body: A healthtech report email has more behind it than a send charge: retained report bytes, recovery records, delivery evidence, and the integration work needed to replace the sender. In an illustrative workload of 10,000 password resets a day, retaining every token digest for 30 days means 300,000 records; a 15-minute validity window represents about 104 unexpired records at a steady arrival rate. Retention dominates the digest count in this example. It does not establish which line dominates your actual bill. Short answer: build secure password reset email around an expiring, hashed token that your database consumes once, then put email sending behind an application-owned contract.

articles.title: Patch Tuesday November 2026: 1,093 fixes, 1 exploited. What to patch first
articles.excerpt: This article first appeared on varaxontech.com, where it is kept up to date. The short version Microsoft released fixes for 1,093 of its own CVEs on 10 November 2026, after a record 1,408 in October.…
articles.body: This article first appeared on varaxontech.com , where it is kept up to date. The short version Microsoft released fixes for 1,093 of its own CVEs on 10 November 2026 , after a record 1,408 in October . Over the last four Patch Tuesdays that is 3,875 CVEs . Only 6 of those 3,875 (0.15%) are on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. None of the 6 was rated Critical by Microsoft. November's one exploited bug, in Outlook, is rated Moderate . If you patched only what Microsoft calls Critical, you would have fixed 297 CVEs and missed all 6 that attackers actually used. A better order: KEV first , then internet-facing systems , then high EPSS , then severity. EPSS put the Outlook bug 7th of 1,093 this month, while its severity label put it near the bottom.

articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

articles.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever
articles.excerpt: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.
articles.body: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.
